entries.test: Public evaluations and technical results showing whether LLMs retain an unavoidable propensity to produce false information would test the claim.
entries.note: The plain reading concerns persistent hallucination risk, not hallucination in every response.

entries.test: Published implementations and reproducibility tests would show whether an LLM can produce deterministic outputs under fixed inputs and execution conditions.

entries.note: “Not anything more” adds an exclusive technical claim to a dismissive comparison. The surrounding passage treats apps and websites as the same mental category.

entries.test: Published AI-agent stories available at publication would show whether any describe capabilities outside code generation, summarization, or generation based on information sources.
entries.note: The universal wording permits testing with counterexamples.
The combined claim includes an allegation of deliberate deception. The separate claim about agents' capabilities could be tested publicly.
There is no shared standard for comparing the intensity of defensiveness, tribalism, and obfuscation across technology revolutions.

entries.test: Public training specifications, system instructions, and interaction tests would show whether LLMs are designed to affirm every user interaction.
entries.note: Design and behavior can be examined without inferring a private motive.
“Digital busyboxes” is a dismissive characterization rather than a defined productivity claim.

entries.test: Public workflow studies measuring human contributions and users' attribution of results would test whether LLM interactions induce users to do most work while crediting AI.
entries.note: The normalization replaces an assertion of persuasive capability with an unqualified outcome.
In context, “artificial intelligence” is a disputed substantive notion of intelligence, not simply the conventional technical category.
The combined proposition lacks shared tests for having thoughts or knowledge. Its performance and cost components could be tested separately.

entries.test: Public deployment documentation and multi-agent evaluations would establish required human setup, supervision, and interference between agents.
entries.note: Requiring substantial setup and supervision does not itself assert that a system has no autonomy.
The normalization drops “for the most part.” “The important parts” has no shared test, especially when responsibility alone counts as doing them.
The source links errors to interpretation based on training data, not solely to lacking knowledge and learning. The downstream failure claim is explicitly a possibility.
“Likely” makes this a probabilistic assertion.

entries.test: Public benchmark validation studies, explanations of practical gains, and evaluations outside coding from the preceding months would test the asserted limitations.
entries.note: “Have unclear results” weakens “nobody can actually explain” and omits the recent-months scope.

entries.test: Published records of the author's research-tool trials and their source materials would show whether the outputs supplied any unique analysis or suggestions.
entries.note: The source specifies the highest-priced RAG/post-RAG tools, not research tools generally. Unpublished trial records could become public evidence.
This asserts adoption in a counterfactual world without the publicity campaign and corporate pressure.
The normalization turns an uncertain counterfactual about excitement into a firm causal assertion. It also retains a private-intention allegation.

entries.test: Contemporaneous marketing claims, documented service restrictions, and public complaints from previously enthusiastic users would test the alleged misleading sales and resulting backlash.
entries.note: The surrounding text identifies the alleged lie as unsustainable service promises.

entries.test: Comparable public evaluations and session records before and after Anthropic's changes would show whether Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Code performance deteriorated.
entries.note: “Appears” introduces an evidence-based observation; it does not merely posit a possible future outcome.

entries.test: Public rental-provider cost and revenue data would show whether Blackwell GPU rentals at $2.75 per GPU-hour cover their costs.
entries.note: This is a conditional statement about present economics, not a conditional forecast.

entries.test: Anthropic's published limits and comparable model evaluations from March and April 2026 would establish whether tighter limits became standard and performance declined.
Public subscription economics and subsequent service histories would show whether paid LLM services are heavily subsidized and degrade during capacity or cost reductions.
entries.note: The source concerns LLM subscriptions and products; “AI subscriptions” broadens that scope.

entries.test: Public financial and service-capacity records would test whether the companies can sustainably deliver their subscriptions at the offered prices and availability.
entries.note: The normalization drops “suggests.” The surrounding passage gives “fundamentally flawed” a concrete economic meaning.

entries.test: Anthropic's uptime and capacity records, subscription commitments, and publicly reported financial projections would test service adequacy and its stated $14 billion burn expectation.
entries.note: The financial component reports an existing expectation, not a forecast that the actual burn will equal it.

entries.test: Public capacity-allocation policies and service changes for existing versus new customers would show whether growth requirements consistently make existing customers bear restrictions first.
entries.note: “Punished” plainly refers here to reduced service or access.

entries.test: Archived ChatGPT limits and public usage records immediately before and after the $100 tier launch would show whether $20 subscribers' limits fell.
Public prices, usage limits, uptime, and performance records during continuing capacity constraints would show whether OpenAI and Anthropic subscription conditions only worsen.
entries.note: The source concerns OpenAI and Anthropic, not AI subscriptions generally. Continuing capacity problems are a stated condition.

entries.test: Public financial disclosures linking purchased capacity, service revenue, and operating costs would test whether added capacity increases losses and services remain economically unsustainable.
Public operating results, service costs, reliability data, and customer retention would test whether LLM reliability and costs prevent economically sustainable AI businesses.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies an economic reading of sustainability.
The normalization omits acquiring customers and attention from the alleged purpose. The intention component cannot be settled by public operating results.

entries.test: Archived Codex rate-limit documentation and service announcements for May 31 and June 1, 2026 would show whether limits were halved.
entries.note: The stated deadline has passed.

entries.test: Public sales promises, service guarantees, disclosed change policies, and actual service histories would show whether customers were misled about predictable long-term quality and availability.
entries.note: “Cannot judge” is stronger than “cannot realistically judge.” The source explicitly leaves intentionality open.
The capacity figures are explicitly presented as guesses.

entries.test: Public revenue, financing, capacity obligations, and liquidity records would show whether each company runs out of money if its stated antecedents occur.
entries.note: The passage gives no deadline for running out of money; 2028 refers to a revenue projection.

entries.test: Subsequent public cost disclosures and rate-limit histories for OpenAI and Anthropic would show whether costs fall or limits are eased.
entries.note: The normalization broadens the claim from the two companies under discussion to AI services generally.

entries.test: Public capacity incidents, model evaluations, and rate-limit changes would show whether both companies reduce service quality or access when capacity limits are reached.
entries.note: The concrete predicted changes provide a plain test despite the emphatic “as much as they can.”
“I imagine” marks speculation. The normalization also assigns the broader enterprise-tier prediction specifically to Anthropic.

entries.test: Public product evaluations and access policies from April through October 2026 would show whether paid generative-AI products materially changed in both quality and availability.
entries.note: More than six months have elapsed, sufficient to assess the ordinary meaning of “mere months.”
The source concerns the labs under discussion, not AI companies generally. “Take as many liberties” and “on the way down” do not specify a shared outcome test.

entries.test: Public subscription revenue and delivery-cost data would show whether the discussed services can become economically sustainable at their current prices and service levels.
entries.note: The normalization expands a claim about the discussed companies' services to AI subscriptions generally.
The passage concerns LLM-based software, not every form of AI. It supplies no shared definition of intelligence.

entries.test: Subsequent subscription prices, usage limits, and documented attempts to run existing workflows would show whether prices rise and rate limits make those workflows impossible.
Public LLM-product sales representations compared with documented capabilities and service economics would test whether every product misrepresents long-term feasibility.
entries.note: A product sold with accurate, candid limitations could refute the universal assertion without establishing anyone's private motive.

entries.test: Public demonstrations and labor-market evidence would show whether LLMs achieve the capabilities and job displacement predicted in the executives' referenced statements.
entries.note: The preceding paragraphs identify the rhetoric being rejected.
This attributes private commercial motives and insincerity to the executives.

entries.test: Public industry responses to documented AI failures would show whether they attribute failures to users' inadequate use of the technology.
entries.note: The wording is sarcastic, but the normalization captures the factual framing allegation made explicit in the next sentence.

entries.test: Public investigative findings, court evidence, and the attacker's documented communications would test whether the industry's AI-threat messaging directly contributed to the attack.
entries.note: A claim about an actual event's causes can be investigated through public evidence.
The source concerns specific acts of violence, not AI-psychosis harms generally. It asserts what could have happened under a counterfactual product design.
